title: Tailscale Automation: CLI, API and Webhooks (2026)
summary: Tailscale automation runs your tailnet from code using scoped credentials, the API, and policy. Complete the setup by building each component in sequence.
body_markdown:
## Stage 3: Webhooks that react to tailnet events


Instead of polling the API, you let the tailnet push events to an endpoint you control, so a device joining or a key expiring reaches a person.


Because it assumes the first two, this stage comes last: events about tagged devices only mean something once tags are reliable, and events about policy changes only matter once policy goes through review.


### Create a Tailscale webhook and choose events


In the admin console, add a webhook with the URL of your receiver and select the event types it should get. Start narrow.


Subscribe first to device-level events such as a new node appearing, a node needing approval, or a node key nearing expiry, because those are the ones people act on.


Subscribing to everything at the start produces a channel the team mutes within a week, and a muted channel is the usual way this stage fails.


When you create the endpoint, Tailscale shows its signing secret, so copy it straight into your secret store. A secret kept anywhere else is one more thing to rotate later.


### Verify Tailscale webhook signatures before trusting payloads


Anyone can post to your receiver, because it is a public URL. Every genuine delivery carries a signature header with a timestamp and a signature computed from that timestamp and the raw request body, using your secret. The receiver should do three things in order:


1. Read the raw body before any JSON parsing, because re-serialising changes the bytes and breaks the match.
2. Recompute the signature with your secret and compare it to the header using a constant-time comparison.
3. Reject the request if the timestamp is too far from the current time, which stops an attacker replaying a captured valid request later.


**Most people skip the timestamp check** . That leaves a receiver that authenticates payloads but accepts old ones indefinitely. Anything that fails a check gets rejected without a body in the response, and nothing downstream runs.


### Receive it with a script or Activepieces


You can get by with a small self-hosted script: one route, the three checks above, then a call out to chat and to your ticketing system.


If you'd rather not run a service, Activepieces can take the webhook trigger and route the event to Slack, email or a ticket. It sits beside Tailscale's own API, auth keys and Git-based policy tooling and replaces none of them.


The signing secret from the previous step is the part worth a second look: Activepieces supports secret managers as part of its enterprise governance set, so credentials are held centrally rather than in each team's scripts.


Secret managers are listed in the enterprise governance feature set, next to SCIM, custom RBAC, SSO/SAML and audit logs, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production. You still need to apply the signature and timestamp checks before any action step.


Read the flow left to right. The tailnet sends a signed request to the receiver, the receiver checks signature and timestamp, and only a request that passes branches to a Slack message and a ticket.


The point is that the verification step sits between the internet and every side effect.


Test it with one real event, such as bringing up a tagged device, and confirm the message and the ticket both appear. A forged request with a bad signature should produce neither.
